contents.html: On October 19, 2017, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) hosted the Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity Colloquium at its Gaithersburg campus to convene stakeholders from across government, industry, international bodies, and academia. The goal was to better understand the concerns and risks associated with the rapidly expanding landscape of connected devices, known as the Internet of Things. Over 220 people participated, with more than 120 in-person attendees; webcast attendees followed the livestream from the US, Canada, Colombia, Israel, and Argentina.
contents.html_ja: 2017 年 10 月 19 日、米国国立標準技術研究所（NIST）は、政府、産業界、国際機関、学術界の関係者を集めて、ゲイサースバーグの敷地内で「Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity Colloquium」を開催しました。目的は、モノのインターネット（IoT）と呼ばれる、急速に拡大する接続機器の領域に関する懸念とリスクをよりよく理解することでした。220 人を超える人々が参加し、そのうち 120 人以上が会場に来場しました。ウェブキャストの視聴者は、米国、カナダ、コロンビア、イスラエル、アルゼンチンからライブ配信を視聴しました。

contents.html: NIST’s Cybersecurity for IoT Program [Program] supports the development and application of standards, guidelines, and related tools to improve the cybersecurity of connected devices and the environments in which they are deployed. By collaborating with stakeholders across government, industry, international bodies, and academia, the Program aims to cultivate trust and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale.
contents.html_ja: NIST の Cybersecurity for IoT Program［本プログラム］は、接続機器および接続機器が展開される環境のサイバーセキュリティを向上させるための標準、ガイドライン、関連ツールの策定と適用を支援しています。本プログラムは、政府、産業界、国際機関、学術界の関係者と連携することで、信頼を育み、世界規模のイノベーションを可能にする環境を促進することを目指しています。

contents.html: The expanding IoT landscape is subject to an equally expanding list of risks, attacks, and corresponding outcomes. As the Program learned through stakeholder outreach, the list of risks is extensive. It includes – but is far from limited to – opportunities for malicious actors to highjack communication channels, change sensor data, access sensitive information, disrupt vital services, and alter signals and data for nefarious purposes. Outcomes vary and may include the collection of bad data, and actual, physical harm. Stakeholders have expressed interest in NIST producing guidelines to help organizations understand and manage cybersecurity and privacy risks associated with the use of IoT.
contents.html_ja: 拡大を続ける IoT の領域は、同様に増え続けるリスク、攻撃、およびそれに伴う結果の影響を受けます。本プログラムが関係者へのアウトリーチを通じて知ったとおり、リスクの一覧は広範です。これには、悪意ある攻撃者が通信チャネルを乗っ取る、センサーデータを改変する、機微な情報にアクセスする、重要なサービスを妨害する、不正な目的で信号やデータを改ざんするといった機会が含まれますが、それらに限りません。結果はさまざまであり、不良データの収集や、実際の物理的な被害が含まれる場合があります。関係者は、組織が IoT の利用に伴うサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクを理解し管理するのに役立つガイドラインを NIST が作成することに関心を示しています。

contents.html: The IoT Cybersecurity Colloquium [Colloquium] focused on challenges organizations face in managing the cybersecurity and privacy risks associated with the Internet of Things. Speakers from industry, academia, international bodies, and government explored the current threat landscape, as well as challenges and considerations specific to the IoT ecosystem. Speakers also discussed practical risk management considerations for IoT deployment, protection, and operation over the course of the device lifecycle.

contents.html: 2.1 Defining the Internet of Things

contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p8の見出し

contents.html: There is no consensus amongst industry on how to define the Internet of Things, which the Colloquium reflected. Some speakers provided a description or scope of IoT, while others left it open-ended. One speaker described IoT as “‘things’ such as devices or sensors – other than computers, smartphones, or tablets – that connect, communicate, or transmit information with or between each other through the internet.” Another speaker said that “devices or things are not full-fledged computers” but are instead “purpose-built items” that “have sensors… can communicate over networks… [and] bridge the physical world with the electronic one.” Furthermore, there was no consensus on whether developing such a definition would be useful. While some thought scoping IoT would have benefits for cybersecurity and privacy discussions (e.g. to determine an organization’s goals), others argued that any set definition would be too limiting in a rapidly evolving field.
contents.html_ja: 産業界には、モノのインターネットをどのように定義するかについての合意はなく、コロキアムもそれを反映していました。登壇者の中には IoT の説明や範囲を示した人もいれば、定めないままにした人もいました。ある登壇者は、IoT を「コンピューター、スマートフォン、タブレット以外の、機器やセンサーなどの『モノ』で、インターネットを通じて、互いに接続し、通信し、または情報を送信するもの」と説明しました。別の登壇者は、「機器やモノは本格的なコンピューターではない」が、むしろ「専用目的の品目」であり、「センサーを備え……ネットワーク上で通信でき……［そして］物理世界と電子世界を橋渡しする」ものだと述べました。さらに、そのような定義を策定することが有益かどうかについても、合意はありませんでした。IoT の範囲を定めることはサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーの議論（たとえば、組織の目標を決めること）にとって利点があると考える人がいる一方で、急速に進化する分野では、どのような固定的な定義も制約が大きすぎると主張する人もいました。

contents.html: The IoT ecosystem poses cybersecurity and privacy risks that extend beyond traditional data security. Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers addressed IoT-specific cybersecurity and privacy risks – including those posed by cyber, physical, and human elements. This section provides an overview of the IoT cybersecurity and privacy risks discussed at the Colloquium.
contents.html_ja: IoT エコシステムは、従来のデータセキュリティを超えて広がるサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクをもたらします。コロキアムを通じて、登壇者は、サイバー、物理、人的要素によってもたらされるものを含め、IoT 特有のサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクを取り上げました。本節では、コロキアムで議論された IoT のサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクの概要を示します。

contents.html: Speakers discussed how the introduction of IoT to networks and infrastructure has changed the cybersecurity and privacy risks organizations are facing, and how managing these cybersecurity and privacy risks has become increasingly difficult for IT security departments.
contents.html_ja: 登壇者は、ネットワークやインフラストラクチャーへの IoT の導入が、組織が直面するサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクをどのように変えたか、またこれらのリスクの管理が IT セキュリティ部門にとってますます困難になっていることについて議論しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p8の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: From a cybersecurity perspective, while once there was only a need to focus on protecting servers and databases from intrusion, CISOs and front-line professionals are now tasked with defeating well-funded attacks that in some cases can cause immediate physical harm. A single enterprise can have hundreds if not thousands of sensors, and monitoring for attacks in real time is resource-intensive. Traditional IT security systems offer very little defense against these cyber-attacks that can shut down power grids, smart traffic systems, and automobiles.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティの観点では、かつてはサーバーやデータベースを侵入から守ることだけに注力すればよかったのに対し、CISO や第一線の専門家は現在、十分な資金を得た攻撃によって、場合によっては直接的な物理的被害を引き起こされる事態を防ぐ任務を負っています。1 つのエンタープライズが数百、場合によっては数千のセンサーを有することがあり、攻撃をリアルタイムで監視するには多くのリソースが必要です。従来の IT セキュリティシステムは、電力網、スマート交通システム、自動車を停止させかねないこうしたサイバー攻撃に対して、ほとんど防御になりません。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p8の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: The ubiquity of IoT devices poses challenges for managing the personal information they collect and helping people understand how that information is processed by a system. IoT can – intentionally or unintentionally – lead to the direct collection of sensitive personal information such as geolocation, financial account numbers, and health information. Many consumers are unaware that devices already in homes can surreptitiously record and process their information. As speakers pointed out, from personal health information on wearables to cameras on baby monitors, consumers have an expectation of privacy that is currently not met.
contents.html_ja: IoT 機器が至る所に存在することは、機器が収集する個人情報を管理し、その情報がシステムでどのように処理されるかを人々が理解できるようにするうえで、課題となります。IoT は、意図の有無にかかわらず、位置情報、金融口座番号、健康情報といった機微な個人情報の直接の収集につながる場合があります。多くの消費者は、すでに家庭にある機器が、自分の情報をひそかに記録し処理する可能性があることを知りません。登壇者が指摘したとおり、ウェアラブル機器の個人の健康情報から、ベビーモニターのカメラに至るまで、消費者はプライバシーへの期待を持っていますが、それは現在満たされていません。

contents.html: When assessing their particular set of risks, an organization must consider the nature of a specific IoT device and how it is being used in order to identify any associated cybersecurity threats or privacy problems. Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers demonstrated that the list of risks is extensive. It includes – but is far from limited to – opportunities for malicious actors to hijack communication channels, spoof sensor data, access sensitive information, disrupt vital services, and alter signals and data for nefarious purposes. Furthermore, while cybersecurity and privacy risks are present and need to be addressed throughout a device’s lifecycle, cybersecurity and privacy are often an afterthought and not considered throughout the system development lifecycle.
contents.html_ja: 組織は、自らに固有のリスクの集合を評価するとき、関連するサイバーセキュリティ上の脅威やプライバシー上の問題を特定するために、特定の IoT 機器の性質と、その使われ方を考慮しなければなりません。コロキアムを通じて、登壇者はリスクが非常に多岐にわたることを示しました。そこには、悪意ある攻撃者が通信チャネルを乗っ取る、センサーデータを偽装する、機微な情報にアクセスする、重要なサービスを妨害する、不正な目的で信号やデータを改ざんするといった機会が含まれますが、それらに限りません。さらに、サイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクは機器のライフサイクル全体にわたって存在し、対処する必要がありますが、サイバーセキュリティとプライバシーは後回しにされがちで、システム開発ライフサイクル全体を通じて考慮されていません。

contents.html: Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers and attendees expressed a need for a framework or other type of guidance for assessing and scoping IoT cybersecurity and privacy risks in order to provide an informed approach to securing devices and the ecosystems in which they are deployed.

contents.html: Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers covered the cybersecurity and privacy challenges posed by a variety of facets of the IoT ecosystem. This section provides an overview of IoT-specific risks discussed during the presentations and conversations, but not a comprehensive review of all IoT cybersecurity and privacy challenges.
contents.html_ja: コロキアムを通じて、登壇者は、IoT エコシステムのさまざまな側面がもたらすサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーの課題を取り上げました。本節では、発表や議論で取り上げられた IoT 特有のリスクの概要を示しますが、IoT のサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーの課題をすべて網羅的に検討するものではありません。

contents.html: 2.3.1 Need for Incentives
contents.html_ja: 2.3.1 インセンティブの必要性
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p9の見出し

contents.html: Speakers indicated that there is a lack of incentives to build cybersecurity and privacy into IoT devices. Cybersecurity is often an afterthought to getting to market, with price and features prioritized. There is also a general lack of consumer education leading to a lack of demand for better cybersecurity and privacy. There are guidelines available to help manufacturers mitigate the risk, but a lack of incentives to adhere to them. Furthermore, there is a communication gap between technical and executive professionals. Speakers noted this gap will likely continue to exist until executives and technical professionals are more aware of the potential consequences of an IoT cybersecurity breach or failure.
contents.html_ja: 登壇者は、IoT 機器にサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーを組み込むためのインセンティブが不足していると指摘しました。市場投入にあたっては価格と機能が優先され、サイバーセキュリティは後回しにされがちです。消費者教育も全般的に不足しており、そのため、より優れたサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーへの需要が生まれていません。製造者がリスクを軽減するのに役立つガイドラインは存在しますが、それに従うインセンティブがありません。さらに、技術の専門家と経営層との間にコミュニケーションの断絶があります。登壇者は、経営層と技術の専門家が、IoT のサイバーセキュリティ侵害や障害がもたらしうる結果をより強く認識するようになるまで、この断絶は続く可能性が高いと述べました。

contents.html: 2.3.2 Sensors
contents.html_ja: 2.3.2 センサー
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p9の見出し

contents.html: Speakers noted that with the rapid proliferation of IoT devices comes a rapid accumulation of data – data that offers a host of insights while also posing a host of security and privacy risks. With such an increase in the volume of data, organizations have to consider how the data is processed. While there are methods for analyzing anomalies in data, it can be difficult to analyze massive amounts of data to find discrepancies in real time (which many IoT applications need), especially when dealing with a sensor attack.
contents.html_ja: 登壇者は、IoT 機器が急速に普及するにつれて、データが急速に蓄積されると述べました。そのデータは、数多くの洞察をもたらす一方で、数多くのセキュリティおよびプライバシーのリスクももたらします。データ量がこれほど増えると、組織はデータの処理方法を考慮しなければなりません。データの異常を分析する方法はありますが、膨大なデータを分析して不整合をリアルタイムで（多くの IoT アプリケーションが必要とします）見つけることは、特にセンサーへの攻撃に対処している場合には、困難になりえます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p9の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: The volume of sensor data can also be used by both attackers and legitimate users to compromise users’ security and privacy. For example, smart meters can be analyzed to learn a person’s TV watching habits; gyroscope orientation can be used to get the password or text from a phone based on how a user’s hand is tilted while typing; and a bad actor can even learn health and religious information from a smart phone GPS location.
contents.html_ja: センサーデータの量は、攻撃者と正当な利用者の双方が、利用者のセキュリティとプライバシーを損なうために利用することもできます。たとえば、スマートメーターを分析して人のテレビ視聴習慣を知ることができます。ジャイロスコープの向きから、入力時のユーザーの手の傾き方に基づいて、電話のパスワードや文字列を得ることができます。さらに、悪意ある行為者は、スマートフォンの GPS 位置情報から、健康や宗教に関する情報を知ることさえできます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p9の画像と照合し一致

contents.html: One of the speakers demonstrated how sensors are now a feasible attack vector, as they are used to understand a physical environment and gather information. This data informs decisions and actions, and any spoofing can lead to unanticipated consequences. A spoofing attack could affect things such as a GPS in a boat, the anti-lock braking system in a car, or a pacemaker located in a human body. Even an attack on a phasor measurement unit, which measures electrical waves, could destabilize portions of a power grid.
contents.html_ja: 登壇者の 1 人は、センサーが物理環境を把握して情報を収集するために使われるため、現在では実行可能な攻撃ベクトルになっていることを実演しました。このデータは判断と行動の根拠となるため、偽装があると予期しない結果につながりかねません。偽装攻撃は、船の GPS、自動車のアンチロックブレーキシステム、人体に埋め込まれたペースメーカーなどに影響を与える可能性があります。電気の波を測定する同期フェーザ測定装置への攻撃でさえ、電力網の一部を不安定にする可能性があります。

contents.html: 2.3.3 Supply Chain
contents.html_ja: 2.3.3 サプライチェーン
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p10の見出し

contents.html: Supply chain threats are a concern in the IoT ecosystem as many manufacturers do not create the entire device. Speakers discussed how manufacturers often use components produced elsewhere, and that these components may be produced by suppliers whose cybersecurity practices are unknown to the manufacturer. Many threats exploit vulnerabilities in IoT components that were acquired via the supply chain during the development, modification, or support of these devices.
contents.html_ja: 多くの製造者は機器全体を自ら作るわけではないため、サプライチェーンの脅威は IoT エコシステムにおける懸念事項です。登壇者は、製造者がしばしば他所で作られた部品を使うこと、そしてそれらの部品が、サイバーセキュリティ慣行が製造者に知られていないサプライヤーによって作られている場合があることを議論しました。多くの脅威は、これらの機器の開発、改変、サポートの際にサプライチェーンを通じて入手された IoT 部品の脆弱性を悪用します。

original_blocks.html: On October 19, 2017, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) hosted the Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity Colloquium at its Gaithersburg campus to convene stakeholders from across government, industry, international bodies, and academia. The goal was to better understand the concerns and risks associated with the rapidly expanding landscape of connected devices, known as the Internet of Things. Over 220 people participated, with more than 120 in-person attendees; webcast attendees followed the livestream from the US, Canada, Colombia, Israel, and Argentina.

NIST’s Cybersecurity for IoT Program [Program] supports the development and application of standards, guidelines, and related tools to improve the cybersecurity of connected devices and the environments in which they are deployed. By collaborating with stakeholders across government, industry, international bodies, and academia, the Program aims to cultivate trust and foster an environment that enables innovation on a global scale.

The expanding IoT landscape is subject to an equally expanding list of risks, attacks, and corresponding outcomes. As the Program learned through stakeholder outreach, the list of risks is extensive. It includes – but is far from limited to – opportunities for malicious actors to highjack communication channels, change sensor data, access sensitive information, disrupt vital services, and alter signals and data for nefarious purposes. Outcomes vary and may include the collection of bad data, and actual, physical harm. Stakeholders have expressed interest in NIST producing guidelines to help organizations understand and manage cybersecurity and privacy risks associated with the use of IoT.

The IoT Cybersecurity Colloquium [Colloquium] focused on challenges organizations face in managing the cybersecurity and privacy risks associated with the Internet of Things. Speakers from industry, academia, international bodies, and government explored the current threat landscape, as well as challenges and considerations specific to the IoT ecosystem. Speakers also discussed practical risk management considerations for IoT deployment, protection, and operation over the course of the device lifecycle.

original_blocks.html: In holding the Colloquium, NIST sought to hear from stakeholders about IoT cybersecurity and privacy concerns, and understand practical cybersecurity and privacy risk management considerations for IoT. To facilitate this, the Program asked attendees to come prepared to share their perspectives on a variety of questions, presented in the “Security and Privacy Considerations for IoT" Pre-Read Essay [Essay].

Video and the slides from each presentation are available on the IoT Cybersecurity Colloquium web page. Based on feedback collected from stakeholders, this report provides a summary of key conversation points and a general discussion of possible follow-on activities for the Program.

The summary below identifies takeaways and observations from the event. It does not necessarily indicate attendees’ unanimous support, nor is it intended to represent all the thoughts, opinions, and suggestions provided during the sessions.

There is no consensus amongst industry on how to define the Internet of Things, which the Colloquium reflected. Some speakers provided a description or scope of IoT, while others left it open-ended. One speaker described IoT as “‘things’ such as devices or sensors – other than computers, smartphones, or tablets – that connect, communicate, or transmit information with or between each other through the internet.” Another speaker said that “devices or things are not full-fledged computers” but are instead “purpose-built items” that “have sensors… can communicate over networks… [and] bridge the physical world with the electronic one.” Furthermore, there was no consensus on whether developing such a definition would be useful. While some thought scoping IoT would have benefits for cybersecurity and privacy discussions (e.g. to determine an organization’s goals), others argued that any set definition would be too limiting in a rapidly evolving field.

The IoT ecosystem poses cybersecurity and privacy risks that extend beyond traditional data security. Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers addressed IoT-specific cybersecurity and privacy risks – including those posed by cyber, physical, and human elements. This section provides an overview of the IoT cybersecurity and privacy risks discussed at the Colloquium.

Speakers discussed how the introduction of IoT to networks and infrastructure has changed the cybersecurity and privacy risks organizations are facing, and how managing these cybersecurity and privacy risks has become increasingly difficult for IT security departments.

From a cybersecurity perspective, while once there was only a need to focus on protecting servers and databases from intrusion, CISOs and front-line professionals are now tasked with defeating well-funded attacks that in some cases can cause immediate physical harm. A single enterprise can have hundreds if not thousands of sensors, and monitoring for attacks in real time is resource-intensive. Traditional IT security systems offer very little defense against these cyber-attacks that can shut down power grids, smart traffic systems, and automobiles.

The ubiquity of IoT devices poses challenges for managing the personal information they collect and helping people understand how that information is processed by a system. IoT can – intentionally or unintentionally – lead to the direct collection of sensitive personal information such as geolocation, financial account numbers, and health information. Many consumers are unaware that devices already in homes can surreptitiously record and process their information. As speakers pointed out, from personal health information on wearables to cameras on baby monitors, consumers have an expectation of privacy that is currently not met.

When assessing their particular set of risks, an organization must consider the nature of a specific IoT device and how it is being used in order to identify any associated cybersecurity threats or privacy problems. Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers demonstrated that the list of risks is extensive. It includes – but is far from limited to – opportunities for malicious actors to hijack communication channels, spoof sensor data, access sensitive information, disrupt vital services, and alter signals and data for nefarious purposes. Furthermore, while cybersecurity and privacy risks are present and need to be addressed throughout a device’s lifecycle, cybersecurity and privacy are often an afterthought and not considered throughout the system development lifecycle.

Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers and attendees expressed a need for a framework or other type of guidance for assessing and scoping IoT cybersecurity and privacy risks in order to provide an informed approach to securing devices and the ecosystems in which they are deployed.

Over the course of the Colloquium, speakers covered the cybersecurity and privacy challenges posed by a variety of facets of the IoT ecosystem. This section provides an overview of IoT-specific risks discussed during the presentations and conversations, but not a comprehensive review of all IoT cybersecurity and privacy challenges.

Speakers indicated that there is a lack of incentives to build cybersecurity and privacy into IoT devices. Cybersecurity is often an afterthought to getting to market, with price and features prioritized. There is also a general lack of consumer education leading to a lack of demand for better cybersecurity and privacy. There are guidelines available to help manufacturers mitigate the risk, but a lack of incentives to adhere to them. Furthermore, there is a communication gap between technical and executive professionals. Speakers noted this gap will likely continue to exist until executives and technical professionals are more aware of the potential consequences of an IoT cybersecurity breach or failure.

Speakers noted that with the rapid proliferation of IoT devices comes a rapid accumulation of data – data that offers a host of insights while also posing a host of security and privacy risks. With such an increase in the volume of data, organizations have to consider how the data is processed. While there are methods for analyzing anomalies in data, it can be difficult to analyze massive amounts of data to find discrepancies in real time (which many IoT applications need), especially when dealing with a sensor attack.

The volume of sensor data can also be used by both attackers and legitimate users to compromise users’ security and privacy. For example, smart meters can be analyzed to learn a person’s TV watching habits; gyroscope orientation can be used to get the password or text from a phone based on how a user’s hand is tilted while typing; and a bad actor can even learn health and religious information from a smart phone GPS location.

One of the speakers demonstrated how sensors are now a feasible attack vector, as they are used to understand a physical environment and gather information. This data informs decisions and actions, and any spoofing can lead to unanticipated consequences. A spoofing attack could affect things such as a GPS in a boat, the anti-lock braking system in a car, or a pacemaker located in a human body. Even an attack on a phasor measurement unit, which measures electrical waves, could destabilize portions of a power grid.

Supply chain threats are a concern in the IoT ecosystem as many manufacturers do not create the entire device. Speakers discussed how manufacturers often use components produced elsewhere, and that these components may be produced by suppliers whose cybersecurity practices are unknown to the manufacturer. Many threats exploit vulnerabilities in IoT components that were acquired via the supply chain during the development, modification, or support of these devices.

Component suppliers often have poor cyber hygiene, and these vulnerabilities are more of an issue than the ingenuity of the attackers. From these vulnerabilities, edge devices, IoT platforms, and the enterprise are all subject to hacking, snooping, and tampering.
A speaker explained that identity is critical to IoT because
Most IoT devices connect to the cloud at some point;
Human control of, and access to, these devices is generally controlled by traditional identity solutions; and
A full-lifecycle approach to identity is needed to govern access to things on the Internet.

Most IoT devices are controlled by traditional identity solutions – most commonly username and password. Because bad actors frequently leverage weak identity management practices to access devices, it is necessary to take a full-lifecycle approach to identity management in the IoT – that is, considering cybersecurity and privacy in every stage of the device lifecycle, from design to deployment to retirement. Furthermore, these devices often come hard-coded with default passwords that cannot be changed.

Analysis of recent attacks reveals that the scale of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks has rapidly increased in recent years. IoT devices are frequently leveraged in these attacks. According to the speakers, there are two types of DDoS attacks: one is a large volume of attacks against the service itself, and the other is a reflection attack where traffic is sent towards a targeted service. This rise is driven, in part, by profitability: this takes the form of bad actors using devices for attacks on individuals’ banking information, as well as people who hire bad actors for espionage and to cause chaos, often making payments with bitcoin and stolen credit cards.

There were also discussions on the role of patching. While patching is important for ongoing device cybersecurity, it is not sufficient. There are too many exploits for patching alone to work, and there is concern about running out of time and money before bad actors do, given how quickly IoT changes.

The Program intends for the document to have broad applicability to address common high-level cybersecurity and privacy risks for IoT, and to introduce practical risk management considerations for IoT product selection, deployment, protection, and operation. As part of the guidance development process, the Program will engage with stakeholders for input. Furthermore, the Program will continue working with the NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence on projects to demonstrate secure and privacy-enhancing IoT solutions.
